The techniques behind the pixels

How Qpunks are made

Every Qpunk is built with real pixel-art craft, not filters.

Drawing techniques

Dithering
Two colors scattered in a pattern to fake shading and texture, the old-school way: skin shadows, fabric.
Outlining
A dark contour around each punk so it pops off the background.
Limited palette
Every trait pulls from a fixed, hand-picked color set, so the whole collection stays coherent.
Gradient backdrops
Smooth color washes behind the character.

Digital effects

Nearest-neighbour upscaling
Built on a tiny 48 px grid, blown up to 3024 px with zero blur, so every pixel stays a crisp square.
CRT glitch and scanlines
Horizontal distortion and pixel offset. The Glitch trait.
Mosaic and censor bars
Pixelated blocks over the eyes. The Mosaic trait.
Starfield shine
Sparkle dots scattered across the frame. The Shine trait.
Seeded build
One seed picks and layers every element, so each punk is unique and fully reproducible.

The lineage is real

The influences

You can point to each one in the art.

Pop Art

Warhol, Lichtenstein

Bold flat color blocks. The dithering dots are a pixel cousin of Lichtenstein's Ben-Day dots. The Pop Riot background is a direct nod.

Graffiti / street art

Basquiat, Banksy

Raw outlines, spray-wall texture, attitude. Lives in Street Wall and Neon Scrawl.

Impasto

Van Gogh

Thick, visible texture. Referenced in Impasto Field, built in pixels through dither layering.

Color field

Rothko

Large flat washes of a single mood color behind the figure. That's the Field backgrounds and the gradient backdrops.

Fauvism

Matisse, Derain

Non-natural, emotional color: blue skin, ember faces. The palettes do exactly this.

Glitch art / vaporwave

The digital-native movement

CRT scanlines, censor bars, chromatic breakup. The Glitch and Mosaic traits.

13 traits, 8 shown on-chain

Built trait by trait

The 8 traits in the on-chain attributes define how a punk looks. The rest shape the mood.

Background
44 hand-made schemes, from Gold Leaf and Blood Canvas to Lagoon Drift and Toxic Moss.
Skin
9 tones, including Pale, Brown, Golden, Ember, Vapor and Undead.
Hair
10 styles (Mohawk, Afro, Buzz, Topknot, Pigtails, Wild…) plus Hair Color.
Eyes
11, including Shades, Laser, Cyclops, Visor, Glow, Stoned, Heart and Patch.
Mouth
10, including Cig, Vape, Fangs, gold Grill, Grin, Tongue and Lips.
Headwear
Beanie, Bucket, Cap, Crown, Halo, Horns, or none.
Body
Hoodie, Jacket, Suit, Tee, Chain.
The mood traits
Head shape, Garment Color, Shine (Starfield, Nova), Glitch (CRT distortion) and Mosaic (censor bars, pixel visors).

No rarity tiers. No piece ranked above another. The only rarity is finding the one that looks back like you.

Before the pixels

How Qpunks started

Qpunks didn't begin as pixels. It began as ink. The first sketches were loose and gestural: single figures built from calligraphic brush strokes, surrounded by blooms of color and dandelion bursts. Just a body, a stance, an attitude on bare paper.

From there it branched into ink figures drawn in one breath, lattice studies where the same figure dissolved onto a warped grid, and big full-bleed abstracts in violent purples, teal and magenta. The question was always the same: how little can a punk be and still read as a punk?

To live as NFTs, as avatars people carry in a wallet, the art needed to be recognizable at thumbnail size and built from traits you could mix. So the ink and the abstractions were distilled into pixels: the same attitude, now sharp, modular and collectible.

The soul stayed. The format grew up.
